Issued at 357 AM CDT Tue Oct 6 2026

A northwest upper flow pattern is forecast to persist over the 
Northern Plains today through Thursday. A progressive shortwave 
moving through Manitoba and Ontario will push a cooler air mass 
into the state from north to south later today through tonight. 
High temperatures today are forecast to range from the upper 60s
north to upper 70s south. Surface high pressure building off 
the Northern Rockies behind a warm front exiting the Red River 
Valley this morning will produce northwest winds around 15 to 20
mph this afternoon, strongest in the far southwest where RH as 
low as 20 percent could yield near-critical fire weather 
conditions. Surface winds relax tonight as the high pressure 
continues to build eastward, but mid to high clouds may prevent 
overnight temperatures from tanking to near-freezing. CAMs show 
that a band of lower to mid level frontogenesis may produce some
light rain showers from north central into northeast North 
Dakota late tonight into Wednesday morning, but a dry low level 
layer of air will likely prevent measurable precipitation at the
surface.

Wednesday will be cooler, but still seasonable with highs in 
the lower 60s to lower 70s. A secondary push of cooler and drier
air will reorient the surface ridge axis from central Alberta 
to southwest North Dakota, resulting in a breezy afternoon for 
the eastern half of the state. The broad surface ridge then 
focuses more squarely over the region Wednesday night, but mid 
to high clouds could once again prevent temperatures from 
falling below freezing. It is likely to be cooler Wednesday 
night than tonight though, with lows mostly in the mid 30s to 
lower 40s. Thursday looks to be less breezy with a similar high 
temperature forecast in the lower 60s to lower 70s as the broad 
surface ridge lingers over the region.

A potent trough digging into British Columbia and the Pacific 
Northwest on Friday will force low amplitude ridging over the 
Northern Plains, quickly transitioning to southwest flow aloft 
as the longwave trough continues deepening along the Pacific 
coast. Ensemble guidance is in good agreement on the phasing of 
synoptic scale features through Friday night, when the heart of 
the low level thermal ridge is forecast to pass through the 
region. Warm air advection commences in time to bring Friday's 
high temperature forecast near 80 in far southwest North Dakota,
with 70s favored for most other parts of the forecast area. 
There is high confidence that a much colder air mass will enter 
the region sometime over the weekend, but the timing of the cold
frontal passage through central North Dakota ranges from as 
early as during the day Saturday (heavily favored by the GEFS) 
to as late as during the day Sunday (an ensemble cluster with 37
percent of the total membership). This lends to large spreads 
in the NBM high temperature distribution on Saturday, with the 
50th percentile maintaining around 60 degrees northwest to near 
80 southeast. That drastically changes on Sunday, when there is 
smaller ensemble spread and higher confidence in daytime maximum
temperatures only in the 40s west and north to 50s south 
central and southeast. High temperatures similar to these remain
in the forecast through Monday, with only a slight warming 
trend thereafter. There will also be a potential for widespread 
sub- freezing temperatures both Sunday and Monday nights.

The NBM increases precipitation chances to around 30 to 60 
percent across much of the area from late Saturday through 
Sunday and into Monday. This lines up well with raw global 
ensemble QPF probabilities. Both sets of guidance favor light 
QPF, with only low to medium chances for exceeding 0.25" over 
any given 24-hour period. This corresponds well to the evident 
uncertainty in the evolution of the western CONUS trough and 
what downstream forcing mechanisms could line up to produce 
appreciable precipitation. A couple ensemble clusters do hint at
a northern stream shortwave cutting off from the western 
trough, and this outcome is likely the most contributive to the 
aforementioned 30 to 60 percent PoPs Sunday into Monday. NBM low
temperatures in the lower to mid 30s Sunday night has allowed a
rain/snow mix to enter the forecast, and that actually 
corresponds well to low NBM probabilities for measurable snow 
that are no greater than 20 percent in the southwest, and no 
greater than 10 percent elsewhere.

Two ensemble clusters constituting 60 percent of the total 
membership keep the base of the longwave trough over the Desert 
Southwest through Tuesday, and a singular cluster with 40 
percent membership favors the trough kicking into the Northern 
and Central Plains around mid week, akin to the 00Z 
deterministic GFS and ECMWF. This outcome could produce a system
with a higher precipitation ceiling, but only for some parts of
the region and with very high probabilities for only rain as a 
precipitation type.
